title: When to Reach for JSONata over json_extract
description: [JSONata](https://jsonata.org/) is an [open query and transformation language for JSON](https://docs.jsonata.org/overview), modelled on XPath. This extension exposes it as a single scalar function that evaluates a JSONata expression against a DuckDB [`JSON`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions.html) value. The real question isn't *what* it can do — it's *when* it earns its keep over DuckDB's native JSON functions, which are the better call for simple access. JSONata wins precisely where a [`json_extract`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions.html) chain stops being concise.

sections.title: JSONata vs. chains of json_extract
sections.description: DuckDB ships a [rich, vectorized JSON function library](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions.html) — [`json_extract`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions.html), [`json_extract_string`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions.html), the [`->`/`->>` operators](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions.html), and the `JSON` type. For one-field-one-path access, those are the right tool and you should not reach for this extension at all. JSONata becomes the better fit once the expression starts to fan out — its single string collapses what native JSON would express as `unnest` plus a subquery.

bulletPoints.label: Array predicate filters
bulletPoints.description: `Phone[type="mobile"].number` selects matching elements *and* projects in one step. The native equivalent extracts the array, `unnest`s it, filters with a `WHERE`, and projects in a correlated subquery.

bulletPoints.label: Object reshaping
bulletPoints.description: An [object-construction](https://docs.jsonata.org/construction) literal builds a fresh JSON object — pulling, renaming, and computing fields together. Natively that's one `json_extract_string` per output field, which gets unwieldy past two or three fields.

bulletPoints.label: Embedded aggregation and higher-order ops
bulletPoints.description: [`$sum`, `$count`, `$max`](https://docs.jsonata.org/aggregation-functions) and [`$map`, `$filter`, `$reduce`](https://docs.jsonata.org/higher-order-functions) operate on arrays *inside* the document, keeping per-row roll-ups inline instead of leaving the JSON value to unnest and re-aggregate.

bulletPoints.label: The break-even
bulletPoints.description: Roughly: any array predicate, any reshape, or more than two output fields tilts toward JSONata. A single field at a fixed path stays simpler in native DuckDB JSON — don't add an extension for it.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: The extension is a scalar UDF — no `ATTACH`, no secrets, no I/O. A call parses the JSONata expression into a program, evaluates it against the supplied [`JSON`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions.html) value, and returns a `JSON` result. The detail that matters most for performance isn't obvious from the signature.

bulletPoints.label: Constant expressions are parsed once
bulletPoints.description: When the expression argument is a SQL constant — by far the common case — the parser runs a single time and the compiled program is reused for every row. Per-row cost is then just the JSON walk plus operator application, not a parse-and-compile on each row, so a static expression over a million rows still parses exactly once.

bulletPoints.label: JSON in, JSON out
bulletPoints.description: Both the input value and the return type are [`JSON`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/json_functions.html). Cast or unnest downstream depending on what the expression yields — `result::VARCHAR`, `result->>'$'`, or `unnest(result::JSON[])` for arrays — exactly like any other DuckDB JSON expression.

bulletPoints.label: Two arities, parse cache intact
bulletPoints.description: The 3-arg form takes a `bindings` JSON object whose keys become `$variable` names inside the expression. This is how you pass per-query values — thresholds, ids, dates — into an otherwise static expression *without* breaking the parse-once optimization, since the expression text stays constant.

sections.title: Scope and caveats
sections.description: The extension wraps the JSONata language faithfully, but it lives inside SQL — the surrounding context is DuckDB, not Node.js. A few things are worth knowing up front.

bulletPoints.label: Single scalar function surface
bulletPoints.description: Everything is reached through one function — there are no helper UDFs for individual JSONata operators. The expression string carries the whole computation. (It is not a JSON loader either; use DuckDB's [`read_json`](https://duckdb.org/docs/data/json/loading_json.html) for that.)

bulletPoints.label: Expressions are SQL strings
bulletPoints.description: JSONata expressions live inside a SQL `VARCHAR` literal, so embedded double quotes need SQL escaping. For long or fiddly expressions, store them in a CTE or a SQL variable and reference by name — and iterate in the official [JSONata exerciser](https://try.jsonata.org/), whose evaluator matches what the extension runs.

bulletPoints.label: No DuckDB-UDF callbacks
bulletPoints.description: JSONata's JavaScript-binding feature isn't wired up — you can't register a DuckDB function as a callable inside the expression. Stick to [JSONata's built-in function library](https://docs.jsonata.org/string-functions).

bulletPoints.label: Per-row cost scales with document and expression size
bulletPoints.description: Deeply-nested documents and complex expressions both cost, and they scale linearly with the data they touch. For very wide rows, materialize the JSONata projection once into a column instead of re-evaluating it in every downstream query.
